title: Urine cell-free RNA for bladder cancer detection and treatment response prediction
abstract:
Nature Medicine, Published online: 02 October 2026; doi:10.1038/s41591-026-04673-3

Applied to samples from more than 600 patients and controls, urinary cell-free RNA profiling with uRARE-seq demonstrated high sensitivity in detecting bladder cancer, and correlated with treatment response.
headline: A urine test can detect bladder cancer and predict how well treatment will work.
why_it_matters: Bladder cancer is often caught late because current screening methods are invasive (requiring a camera inserted into the bladder). A simple urine test could enable earlier detection, which typically leads to better outcomes. Additionally, knowing in advance whether a patient's treatment will work could help doctors adjust therapy faster.
key_findings: Researchers found RNA fragments (genetic material) floating freely in urine that reliably identify patients with bladder cancer versus healthy controls.
The test, called uRARE-seq (a method to read specific RNA patterns in urine), showed high sensitivity — meaning it correctly identifies most cancer cases without many false alarms.
The RNA signatures in urine also predicted which patients would respond well to treatment and which would not, before therapy began.
The findings held up across more than 600 patients and control subjects, suggesting the test is robust and could be widely applicable.
methods_snapshot: Researchers analyzed urine samples from over 600 people using uRARE-seq, a molecular technique that detects and profiles RNA fragments. They compared RNA patterns between bladder cancer patients, cancer-free controls, and patients undergoing treatment to see if the genetic signatures could predict cancer presence and treatment success.

glossary.definition: Fragments of genetic material released into body fluids (like urine) when cells die or release material; found naturally in everyone, but patterns differ in disease.
A laboratory technique that identifies and measures specific RNA patterns present in urine samples.
The ability of a test to correctly identify people who actually have the disease (the opposite of false negatives).
A measurable biological signal (like RNA or a protein) in blood or urine that indicates disease presence or treatment response.
Reading the full set of genetic instructions (RNA) present in a sample to understand what genes are active.

ml_angle: Likely used machine learning algorithms to identify which RNA patterns best separate cancer patients from healthy controls and predict treatment response, though specifics are not detailed in the abstract.
limitations: The study is primarily observational and focused on one cancer type; real-world validation in routine clinical settings is still needed. It's unclear whether the test performs equally well across all bladder cancer subtypes or patient demographics.
